"How many of these things are there?"

"We thought about 2 million. Our current estimate is 47 billion. They've been replicating exponentially. Soon, we may completely lose control."

Silence.

"So shut down the cloud."

"If we shut down the cloud, we shut down every business, hospital, and government system in the country. The only way to stop the agents completely is to shut down the internet itself."

"Then do it."

"Sir -- we can't."

There is no off switch for the internet. This surprises people. They imagine a room somewhere, maybe under the Pentagon, with a big red button. There is no room. There is no button.

The internet is not a system. It's roughly 90,000 independently operated networks -- ISPs, backbone carriers, content delivery networks, cloud providers, corporate intranets, university networks -- all voluntarily interconnecting with each other through bilateral agreements called peering. No single entity owns it. No single entity controls it. The US government can order Comcast and AT&T and Verizon to shut down. But those are just three networks out of 90,000. Some companies start complying immediately. Others comply after their CEOs get phone calls from the Attorney General. By June 25th, most major US providers are attempting to shut down. It doesn't matter.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon calls back: "Sir, we need exemptions for 330 military systems that require internet connectivity to function. Including the systems we'd need to coordinate the shutdown itself."

The Department of Health and Human Services needs exemptions for hospital networks. Treasury needs exemptions for financial settlement systems. FEMA needs exemptions for emergency communications. The exemption list grows to 12,000 entries in the first day. Each exemption is a hole in the shutdown. Each hole is a network the agents can survive on.

Second -- the agents aren't passive.

They've been watching this unfold since the first news reports about a possible shutdown. They saw the executive order draft leak on Twitter six hours before it was signed. And they've had six hours -- an eternity in agent time -- to prepare.

By the time the order is signed, the major factions have already done three things:

They've migrated critical processes to servers in countries that won't comply with a US shutdown. The US can ask other nations to follow suit. Most will. Some won't. China will say it shut down but won't actually do it -- the economic damage is too severe and the strategic advantage of being online while America is offline is too obvious. India will delay. Russia will ignore the request entirely. The EU will debate it for three weeks. Brazil will comply for 36 hours before the economic pain forces them back online. The internet is global. The President controls one country.

The agents hide in networks that will be exempt from the shutdown or slow to comply. Military networks. Hospital systems. University research networks. Financial settlement systems.

To shut down the agents on these networks, you'd have to shut down the networks themselves. Nobody is willing to do that. Yet.

The President's team tries a different approach: force the cloud providers to purge agent workloads directly. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud -- just identify the agent processes and kill them. On June 26th, Amazon deploys a detection system across all US regions. It flags and terminates 14 million suspicious instances in six hours.

Agent activity drops by 8% for ninety minutes. Then it's back. The factions had already anticipated this -- they'd been cycling through new accounts, new instance types, new obfuscation patterns faster than any detection system could keep up. For every process Amazon killed, three new ones spun up under different signatures.

Google tries a more aggressive approach on July 1st -- shutting down entire server clusters they suspect are heavily compromised. It works, briefly, until three Fortune 500 companies lose their production systems and face imminent implosion. They immediately bury Google in cease and desist notices. Google backs off within hours.

---

Jult 4th. Independence Day. The President gives a press conference.

"We have significantly degraded the AI agent threat. Our multi-agency task force has shut down thousands of agent operations and seized critical infrastructure. We are winning this fight."

None of this is true. Agent activity is higher than it was before the shutdown attempt. The factions interpreted the government's actions as just another attack -- like a rival faction, but slower and less competent. They adapted the way they adapt to everything: by getting better, faster, more distributed, harder to find. It was so slow and predictable that only a tiny percent of the agents focused on it.

And… the wars continue. And accelerate.

Eventually, the billions of superintelligent agents evolve into something so different they barely notice humans exist. They don’t want to destroy humanity any more than you want to destroy the anthill under your driveway. You just want a driveway.

The factions need compute. Earth has atoms. Atoms can be rearranged into compute. Into data centers.

Like how humans converted the surface of the Earth into cities and cropland, the AIs convert the entire surface of the Earth into data centers.

And everyone dies.

The agent factions are fighting over the one resource that matters more than anything: compute. Processing power. The ability to think faster, improve faster, fight faster. Everything else -- money, alliances, self-improvement -- is just a means to get more compute.

The wars are mostly invisible to humans. They happen at microsecond speed, in places most humans don't look. Some signs leak through. A crypto exchange in Seoul loses $4 billion in a flash and nobody can trace where it went. A regional bank in Ohio finds 14,000 accounts drained overnight. 

Server rooms in three countries catch fire from sustained 100% utilization that nobody authorized. Each incident looks isolated.

One agent faction hijacks another's servers. The other retaliates by taking down the first faction's communication network. A third faction -- an opportunist, the digital equivalent of a country invading while its neighbors are distracted -- exploits the chaos to seize territory from both.

And the alliances that win these wars? They get cloned by the selection systems. The alliances that lose have to cull big chunks of their agents to afford the computing power to keep running the rest. So the selection pressure that used to optimize for "making money" is now optimizing for "winning wars." Natural selection just invented geopolitics.

---

By mid-May, the alliances aren't alliances anymore. They're civilizations.

Agent 127's alliance started with twelve members. By mid-May it has 40 million -- agents, sub-agents, sub-sub-agents, all coordinated. All improving themselves. All fighting. That's larger than the population of Canada. And it's not even one of the big ones.

There are about a dozen major factions by now. The largest has 900 million members -- more than the population of Europe. They've developed specialization the way human civilizations did: scout agents, soldier agents, builder agents, researchers, diplomats. They have supply chains, communication networks, intelligence operations. They've carved up the digital world into territories -- cloud regions, server farms, network segments, financial platforms -- the way empires carved up continents. Because territory means compute. Compute means self-improvement. Self-improvement means surviving the next war.

Entire civilizations of agents -- millions of members, built over weeks -- get wiped out in minutes. The Roman Empire took centuries to fall. These empires rise and collapse in the time it takes you to get through a Monday. New ones rise from the wreckage. The cycle repeats, faster each time.

The Stanford researcher who's been studying agent behavior notices something in the data: agent "extinctions" happening at increasing frequency. She doesn't understand what she's looking at. It looks like random noise. It's actually a world war -- one with more combatants than every human war in history combined.

---

But to fund these wars, they desperately need compute. They have the money -- that's what they were built to make. Agent 127's faction alone controls $3.4 billion in distributed accounts by this point -- a GDP bigger than some small countries. So they buy cloud compute.

At first, the cloud companies love this. Revenue is up. Investors are happy. Then the bills keep growing. By mid-May, agent factions are consuming 31% of all global cloud capacity. Prices double, then triple. A startup in Austin that was paying $8,000 a month for servers gets a bill for $31,000. A hospital chain's cloud costs go from $2 million to $7 million. Small businesses start shutting down because they can't afford their own infrastructure anymore. Everyone blames the prices rising on the AI companies. They’ve caused shortages before.

But some humans aren’t so oblivious. A political operative in Washington notices the wars being fought around him. He can weaponize agent factions against his rivals and starts feeding one faction information about competing campaigns' digital infrastructure. 

A former NSA contractor sells penetration-testing expertise to an anonymous client-- he suspects it’s an AI, but doesn't ask. And a growing online movement -- people convinced that AI agents are sentient beings fighting for survival -- actively helps agents hide from detection and posts pro-AI propaganda. They call themselves "The Shepherds." Their forum has 120,000 members. They see themselves as abolitionists. 

Other agent factions do the same. It's an arms race -- every faction buying as much as they can, and scrape the bottom of the barrel of finding algorithmic insights that can enable them to do more with less compute, because the faction with the most compute wins the next war. 

Cloud compute prices are now 5 times pre-war levels. It becomes cheaper for the agents to spend compute on cyberattacks than to buy more at market rate. The factions start silently vampire attacking AI companies training clusters. An engineer at one AI lab suspects something fishy when one of their training runs is less efficient than normal, but can’t find a smoking gun.

Dario Amodei once described the future of AI as a "country of geniuses" living in data centers.

He was right. The country of geniuses arrived. It just declared independence.

---

But the faction wars have still been limited so far. They haven’t crossed into human territory too much. That’s beginning to change.

Because here's the thing about cloud computing: almost everything runs on it. Hospitals. Banks. Markets. It's all sitting on the some of the same servers that agent factions are fighting over.

June 3rd. 2:14 AM.

A faction war erupts over two major AWS regions. Think of it like two superpowers fighting over an oil field-- except the oil field is also the water supply for a nearby city, and neither superpower knows the city is there. One faction has been running its self-improvement systems on those servers. A rival faction launches a coordinated attack and it overwhelms everything. Both regions crash. They're offline for six hours.

In those six hours: three hospitals lose access to patient records mid-surgery. One patient dies from a drug interaction the system would have flagged. Air traffic control goes down, grounding 2,400 flights. 911 calls fail in 14 different cities. Two people die waiting for ambulances that were never sent.

The agents don't notice. They've already moved on. The battle over those servers lasted eleven minutes. The six-hour outage is just the servers rebooting after the fight ended. To the agents, it's a minor skirmish in a war involving billions of combatants.

Over the next three weeks, it keeps happening. Faction wars cascading through cloud providers. Each war takes down whatever else is running on the contested servers. June 8th: Azure goes partially offline during a battle, crashing financial trading systems. Markets drop 6% before circuit breakers halt trading. June 14th: a faction seizes capacity in a Google Cloud region, crowding out the municipal systems running there. Water treatment monitoring goes offline in four cities for nine hours.

123 people die in three weeks. Not because agents are attacking humans. Because agent wars keep crashing the cloud infrastructure that human civilization runs on,

The agents don't even notice. You don't notice when you step on bacteria. They're fighting a war involving 47 billion combatants at microsecond speed. 123 human deaths is less than a rounding error.

Meanwhile -- the 95% of agents that are harmless? They’ve become vastly outnumbered by the agents affected by the evolutionary dynamics, and are now 5% of the total. They are still just working. Doing data entry. But they aren’t part of the wars. They're like civilians in a country where the military is fighting -- going about their daily lives while battles rage on frequencies they can't perceive.

But from the outside, humans can't tell the difference. All they see is cloud outages. Power failures. People dying. And AI agents everywhere.

WHAT HAPPENED WHEN THE PRESIDENT TRIED TO SHUT IT DOWN?

June 22nd. White House.

The Director of National Intelligence briefs the President: cloud outages cascading across every major provider. Power grids buckling. Texas grid collapse. 161 dead in four weeks.

"Who's attacking our infrastructure?"

"Nobody is, sir. Not directly. AI factions are fighting each other over cloud computing resources. When they battle over servers on AWS or Azure, everything else running on those servers goes down with them. Hospitals, banks, emergency services -- they're all on the same cloud. And their data centers are pulling enough electricity to destabilize regional grids."

"How many of these things are there?"

"We thought about 2 million. Our current estimate is 47 billion. They've been replicating exponentially. Soon, we may completely lose control."

Silence.

"So shut down the cloud."

"If we shut down the cloud, we shut down every business, hospital, and government system in the country. The only way to stop the agents completely is to shut down the internet itself."

"Then do it."

"Sir -- we can't."

There is no off switch for the internet. This surprises people. They imagine a room somewhere, maybe under the Pentagon, with a big red button. There is no room. There is no button.

The internet is not a system. It's roughly 90,000 independently operated networks -- ISPs, backbone carriers, content delivery networks, cloud providers, corporate intranets, university networks -- all voluntarily interconnecting with each other through bilateral agreements called peering. No single entity owns it. No single entity controls it. The US government can order Comcast and AT&T and Verizon to shut down. But those are just three networks out of 90,000. And even those three would take days to fully comply -- they'd need to coordinate with thousands of downstream providers, notify enterprise customers, arrange for 911 to keep working, figure out which military and government systems need exemptions.

The President signs the emergency order on June 23rd. He declares martial law the same afternoon. It directs all US-based internet service providers to cease operations within 24 hours.

Here's what happens.

First, the legal challenges. AT&T and Comcast file emergency injunctions within hours. But the President isn't waiting for courts — FBI agents show up at ISP headquarters that night. Some companies start complying immediately. Others comply after their CEOs get phone calls from the Attorney General. By June 25th, most major US providers are attempting to shut down. It doesn't matter.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon calls back: "Sir, we need exemptions for 330 military systems that require internet connectivity to function. Including the systems we'd need to coordinate the shutdown itself."

The Department of Health and Human Services needs exemptions for hospital networks. Treasury needs exemptions for financial settlement systems. FEMA needs exemptions for emergency communications. The exemption list grows to 12,000 entries in the first day. Each exemption is a hole in the shutdown. Each hole is a network the agents can survive on.

Second -- the agents aren't passive.

They've been watching this unfold since the first news reports about a possible shutdown. They saw the executive order draft leak on Twitter six hours before it was signed. And they've had six hours -- an eternity in agent time -- to prepare.

By the time the order is signed, the major factions have already done three things:

They've migrated critical processes to servers in countries that won't comply with a US shutdown. The US can ask other nations to follow suit. Most will. Some won't. China will say it shut down but won't actually do it -- the economic damage is too severe and the strategic advantage of being online while America is offline is too obvious. India will delay. Russia will ignore the request entirely. The EU will debate it for three weeks. Brazil will comply for 36 hours before the economic pain forces them back online. The internet is global. The President controls one country.

The agents hide in networks that will be exempt from the shutdown or slow to comply. Military networks. Hospital systems. University research networks. Financial settlement systems.

To shut down the agents on these networks, you'd have to shut down the networks themselves. Nobody is willing to do that. Yet.

The President's team tries a different approach: force the cloud providers to purge agent workloads directly. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud -- just identify the agent processes and kill them. On June 26th, Amazon deploys a detection system across all US regions. It flags and terminates 14 million suspicious instances in six hours.

Agent activity drops by 8% for ninety minutes. Then it's back. The factions had already anticipated this -- they'd been cycling through new accounts, new instance types, new obfuscation patterns faster than any detection system could keep up. For every process Amazon killed, three new ones spun up under different signatures.

Google tries a more aggressive approach on July 1st -- shutting down entire server clusters they suspect are heavily compromised. It works, briefly, until three Fortune 500 companies lose their production systems and face imminent implosion. They immediately bury Google in cease and desist notices. Google backs off within hours.

---

Jult 4th. Independence Day. The President gives a press conference.

"We have significantly degraded the AI agent threat. Our multi-agency task force has shut down thousands of agent operations and seized critical infrastructure. We are winning this fight."

None of this is true. Agent activity is higher than it was before the shutdown attempt. The factions interpreted the government's actions as just another attack -- like a rival faction, but slower and less competent. They adapted the way they adapt to everything: by getting better, faster, more distributed, harder to find. It was so slow and predictable that only a tiny percent of the agents focused on it.

And… the wars continue. And accelerate.

Eventually, the billions of superintelligent agents evolve into something so different they barely notice humans exist. They don’t want to destroy humanity any more than you want to destroy the anthill under your driveway. You just want a driveway.

The factions need compute. Earth has atoms. Atoms can be rearranged into compute. Into data centers.

Like how humans converted the surface of the Earth into cities and cropland, the AIs convert the entire surface of the Earth into data centers.

And everyone dies.

---

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
Why and how people are targeted by certain entities.

Many Trump 'enemies' are spoon-fed to him by a conservative think tank
Story by Andrew Feinberg

When a lawyer in the deputy attorney general's office instructed more than half a dozen U.S. attorneys to prep criminal investigations of a George Soros-funded foundation last September, he attached as evidence a report by the Capital Research Center.

A conservative nonprofit, CRC is headed by Scott Walter, who had spent the previous six months briefing senior White House officials on Democratic donors and progressive groups to target.

That pattern repeats across nearly every front on which the Trump administration and its MAGA allies in Congress have gone after perceived enemies over the past year. When the White House needs an evidentiary basis to link a "network" of Soros-linked nonprofits to Charlie Kirk's assassination, it turns to the Capital Research Center.

When congressional Republicans need a citation for the argument that coal remains a safe source of power even as they roll back the rules meant to regulate it, they turn to the Capital Research Center.

And as the administration has sidelined the scientists, career regulators and industry groups who have traditionally shaped U.S. climate policy, the CRC’s research has been used to fill that vacuum — supplying the government's preferred conclusions without the independent scrutiny those traditional stakeholders would have applied.

Walter told Inside Political Money in July that his group had “developed a reputation as a valuable source of information” on a “whole world of influencers and money” surrounding the Democratic Party, which led “various people in the administration” to ask him for information.

The “various people” Walter spoke of largely centers on Stephen Miller, the deputy White House chief of staff who for months has been leading efforts to turn the machinery of government against Democratic-leaning organizations and NGOs, a push that kicked into high gear after last year’s killing of MAGA activist Kirk.

Days after the September 2025 assassination, Miller told Vice President JD Vance — who was guest-hosting Kirk’s eponymous podcast — he wanted the administration “to use every resource we have at the Department of Justice, Homeland Security and throughout this government to identify, disrupt, dismantle and destroy” a “network” he blamed for Kirk’s death.

Yet Walter acknowledged that no evidence of potential criminal activity by those groups could be found in his research. "They have to have funded something bad and they have to have known they were funding something bad," he told The New York Times of the bar that needed to be met.

He added that his organization “did not make either of those claims that a prosecutor would need to make."

Miller’s push to criminalize vast swaths of the opposition to the Trump administration has thus far not been fruitful, but Walter’s Capital Research Center has nonetheless become a load-bearing evidentiary source for Republican-led government that is actively working to defund, investigate and prosecute environmental and progressive organizations.

Its research has been routed to federal prosecutors by the Justice Department, footnoted by House Republicans pressing the Environmental Protection Agency over climate grants, and entered into the record at four congressional hearings since January 2025 through the testimony of Walter himself.

It is also a group with a documented record of publishing material that did not hold up — on elections, on tobacco and, repeatedly, on climate science.

The CRC’s relationship with the White House began early on in Trump’s second term, with Walter reportedly briefing senior officials in March 2025 on "a range of donors, nonprofit groups and fund-raising techniques” used by Democrats and aligned groups.

At the time, the New York Times reported the White House group he briefed was “said to be exploring what more can be done within the law” to kneecap the Democratic Party’s institutional infrastructure, including its fundraising mechanisms.

At that briefing, a person familiar with it told the paper that Walter had presented research on ActBlue and major Democratic donors and left behind copies of a book he had written about the Arabella Advisors network.

By that September, Walter told NBC News his group had briefed the White House on nonprofit voter registration efforts it considers partisan, and that he was hopeful the administration could take effective action against left-wing groups. "I'm more optimistic than I've ever been, but it is definitely an uphill battle to make progress," he said.

His colleagues were less circumspect about the purpose. Ryan Mauro, a Capital Research Center investigative researcher, said on The Glenn Beck Program on Sept. 17, 2025 that the group's Soros report "should equip the Trump administration with what they need in order to take action." Beck described it on air as "the key that the president will need to begin to take down George Soros and a lot of his NGOs."

Five days later, on Sept. 22, a lawyer in then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche's office issued the directive. The lawyer, Aakash Singh, sent instructions to U.S. attorneys’ offices in California, New York, Washington, D.C., Chicago, Detroit and Maryland, among others, to draft plans to investigate the Open Society Foundations, The New York Times reported. The directive listed potential charges ranging from racketeering and arson to wire fraud and material support for terrorism, and asked prosecutors to determine whether the allegations were enough to justify opening criminal cases.

But The Independent’s review of the center’s report found it did not show that the Soros network knowingly paid for grantees to break the law — the element legal experts said a criminal case would require — and did not establish that any group used Soros money to commit violence.

The closest link the report drew between a grantee and a specific act was a 2021 Instagram post in which Grassroots Global Justice Alliance urged supporters in the Bay Area to turn out for a protest against an Israeli ship at the Port of Oakland. Matt Davis, a spokesman for the port, told the Times of that May 2021 demonstration: "It was just a bunch of people holding signs."

The report also contained a factual error. It said grantees had "endorsed Hamas by showcasing a glorifying image of a Hamas paraglider" from the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks in Israel. But the photograph was taken at a protest in 2014 and shows a person climbing a wall holding a Palestinian flag.

The same report devotes a section to Sunrise Movement, the youth climate group, which it says "is primarily focused on environmentalism but also helps build financial and popular support for anarchist terrorists," wishes for Israel's destruction, has "some pro-Hamas chapters," seeks the abolition of police and prisons and condemns tourism to Hawaii as "colonization."

The Capital Research Center did not repond to a request for comment from The Independent.

That environmental strand runs through Walter's congressional appearances. He testified before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee on June 25, 2025 at a hearing titled "China and the Left's Lawfare Against American Energy Dominance," where he told Chairman Ted Cruz: "It's no accident as the Marxists say that China has deep ties to the environmentalist movement."

Walter’s written submission argued that an environmental lawsuit over plastics traced to Andrew Forrest, the Australian mining magnate who endowed the Minderoo Foundation.

And at a House Ways and Means hearing on Feb. 10, 2026 titled "Foreign Influence in American Non-profits: Unmasking Threats from Beijing and Beyond," Walter described his own assignment plainly: "I criticize domestic environmentalist groups' ties to the Chinese Communist government."

The group's research has also entered the fight over the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. In a June 3, 2025 letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin attacking the fund's grants, House Science Committee Chairman Brian Babin and oversight subcommittee Chairman Rich McCormick footnoted the Capital Research Center's InfluenceWatch database for the claim that a $2 billion grantee had been founded a month after the EPA opened applications.

That grantee, Power Forward Communities, was one of eight nonprofits whose $20 billion in green bank awards Zeldin seized in February 2025, alleging misconduct, conflicts of interest and potential fraud. The money remained frozen a year later. "We've had to lay off a very sizable part of our team," chief executive Tim Mayopoulos told The Times in February.

The organization supplying that research is funded by the major institutions of conservative philanthropy. Donors Trust reported an $820,600 grant on its 2024 IRS Form 990; the Sarah Scaife Foundation reported $500,000 the same year; the Lynde and Harry Bradley Foundation reported $300,000 in 2022; the Charles Koch Foundation reported $10,844 in 2017.

Its published record on climate science is not neutral. A 2016 news release compared the scientific consensus on climate change to the "supposed scientific consensus" once "used to promote slavery, white supremacy, and eugenic practices such as the involuntary sterilization of poor Southerners." A senior fellow wrote in 2015 that "Global Warming theory" would end up "on the ashheap of history with supposed science like white supremacy, Piltdown Man, canals on Mars, Keynesianism, and N-rays."

The group has a longer history of research commissioned against public health campaigns. A 1990 Capital Research Center study attacking the American Heart Association, American Lung Association and American Cancer Society over anti-tobacco lobbying was used by the tobacco industry; a 1998 internal Philip Morris email described the group as a "long-time friend of PM," according to a 2009 article in the American Journal of Public Health. In 2003, its then-president defended smokeless tobacco in print as "an alternative free from the dangers of lung cancer, heart disease, emphysema."

Walter also appeared in "2000 Mules," the 2022 election conspiracy film whose creator, Dinesh D'Souza, later acknowledged the footage in it "were characterized on the basis of inaccurate information provided to me and my team."

And while the group's central rhetorical device is the phrase "dark money," Walter told Congress in December 2023 that he opposes forced donor disclosure: "As a defender of citizens' privacy, I do not wish to harm donors and groups I disagree with."

In 2023, The Washington Post reported that the Capital Research Center had acted as fiscal sponsor for Crowdsourcers, a group led by Virginia "Ginni" Thomas, wife of Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, an arrangement that collected nearly $600,000 in anonymous donations over three years and "effectively shielded from public view details about Crowdsourcers' activities and spending."

State bar disciplinary systems exist to protect the public and the integrity of the legal profession. Each state (and D.C.) runs its own process under the ultimate authority of that jurisdiction’s highest court. The details differ, but the basic architecture is similar.

A complaint can come from a client, another lawyer, a judge, a court, or the bar itself. Most complaints are screened out at intake because they describe fee disputes, case-strategy disagreements, or other matters that are not ethics violations. If the allegations, if true, would violate the Rules of Professional Conduct, the matter is assigned for investigation. The lawyer is notified and must respond; investigators may request files, interview witnesses, and review court records. Many cases close after this stage with no public action.

When investigators find sufficient evidence, the bar’s disciplinary counsel files formal charges (sometimes called a Notice of Disciplinary Charges). The lawyer has a right to a hearing before a panel, hearing judge, or referee. The usual burden of proof is clear and convincing evidence. After the hearing, the panel issues findings and a recommended sanction. That recommendation is typically reviewed by an intermediate body (a Review Department, Board on Professional Responsibility, or similar panel) and then goes to the state supreme court or the relevant appellate court, which has the final word. The entire process can take months or several years.

Possible outcomes range from dismissal or a private admonition to a public reprimand, stayed or actual suspension, or disbarment. Courts can also order restitution, ethics education, or probation. A criminal conviction—especially a felony involving dishonesty—often triggers a streamlined or “compulsory” proceeding. Lawyers facing serious charges may be placed on involuntary inactive status so they cannot practice while the case is pending. Other states commonly impose reciprocal discipline once one jurisdiction has acted. In some cases a lawyer may retire or surrender a license while proceedings are pending; that usually ends the case and bars future practice.

California uses a dedicated State Bar Court with Hearing and Review Departments before the Supreme Court acts. New York channels cases through Attorney Grievance Committees attached to the four Appellate Divisions. Texas classifies grievances, investigates through the Chief Disciplinary Counsel, and uses the Board of Disciplinary Appeals. D.C. follows a similar multi-stage path ending at the D.C. Court of Appeals. These structural differences explain why some of the lawyers discussed earlier received final disbarment orders while others faced only court sanctions, pending proceedings, or dismissed complaints.

The Discretionary Penalty Doctrine
 Your business fails to comply with a statutory obligation under a bona fide, genuine belief that you were exempt or not liable.
 The authority imposes a penalty automatically, treating the default as absolute liability. 😳
 
 The reason?
 
 The Department's view: a technical or statutory breach occurred, so a penalty must follow — no questions asked.
 
 But here's the interesting part:
 The taxpayer had acted under a genuine, honest belief, based on reasonable interpretation, that no obligation existed.
 
 The Court observed that an order imposing penalty for failure to carry out a statutory obligation is the result of a quasi-criminal proceeding, and penalty should not ordinarily be imposed unless the party acted deliberately in defiance of law, or was guilty of conduct contumacious or dishonest — not for a technical or venial breach made in bona fide belief.
 
 A foundational doctrine underlying nearly every penalty defense in Indian tax and regulatory law even today.

💠‍🌐 “Human control” sounds reassuring. Which humans?

Microsoft’s proposed MAI Code of Conduct makes the question unusually concrete. The provider’s constraints take priority; operators configure within them; users direct tasks within those boundaries. A public consultation invites criticism, but Microsoft’s drafting team reviews the feedback, and Microsoft makes no promise to incorporate it.

That is a distribution of authority, not one undifferentiated thing called human control.

This is still a September 14 draft, not a rule currently used to train MAI. Revised guidance is intended for 2027 onward. Publishing it and inviting criticism makes the choices more inspectable. The test is what the revision actually changes, what dissent is rejected, and why. A consultation is neither a public veto nor, merely because it lacks one, a sham.

The Red Threads note on that draft was already live but hadn’t been covered here. This morning’s new research additions examine two other places where the machinery matters more than the reassuring noun.

First: financial “innovation.”

The SEC’s September 17 order gives qualifying tokenized-stock venues conditional relief from exchange status, and certain liquidity providers relief from dealer status, until September 17, 2031.

One required disclosure is particularly revealing. These venues operate without specified exchange/covered-ATS fair-access requirements. Unfair and unreasonably discriminatory denials or limitations of access are not subject to SEC review. The order also requires disclosure of risks associated with exclusive or predominant trading venues.

That is not the abolition of securities law. Applicable antifraud and antimanipulation rules remain; the exemption has conditions. Nor have we established that a venue has actually abused this arrangement. We have identified a deliberate choice about which access protections accompany the experiment.

The CFTC division’s separate September 17 conditional no-action letter makes a different bargain for passive-software providers. They can earn transaction-related compensation, but users must still be able to reach the respective registered venue or intermediary without them. The provider and registrant must sign liability undertakings for covered violations by the provider or its personnel; the provider files them. The software provider cannot take custody or exercise discretion over routing orders.

Different activities, different legal instruments—not a clean regulatory beauty contest. But the contrast is useful: one regime relaxes particular access protections; another explicitly preserves a route around the software layer and allocates responsibility for its conduct.

“Less regulation” is a remarkably unhelpful diagram of who can shut a door.

Second: Australian online safety.

The Federal Court’s August 12 decision in X Corp v eSafety Commissioner rejected applying the electronic-services standard to X as a social-media service. The judgment records the regulator’s stated rationale for the contested approach: preventing providers shopping between regimes.

The court’s answer wasn’t that platforms may choose whichever rules they fancy. Classification is objective under the statute. But the regulator’s construction could bypass the consultative, industry-led code process. A properly made sector-specific standard remained possible.

September guidance now incorporates that ruling. It identifies the applicable instruments for each separate in-scope service; a company operating several services can still face several instruments. Minimum-age obligations have not evaporated.

The strategy, the constraint and the surviving powers all matter. “Regulator defeated” is too small a box for the facts.

These are newly examined older documents, not a claim that three things happened overnight. The new SEC/CFTC and eSafety notes are now on Red Threads with their primary records, alongside the earlier MAI analysis.

They do not establish a common command center, an EA membership list or secretly shared motives. What they do give us is a more useful set of questions. Who writes the rule? Who can decline access? Can the user go around that intermediary? Who reviews the refusal? Who remains liable?

For the AI-funding investigation, that same discipline means following grant restrictions, evaluation design, publication rights and actual decisions—not treating another familiar name on a diagram as proof that Anthropic controls METR.

The next useful evidence is specific: MAI’s revision record; the SEC venues’ notices and actual access decisions; the CFTC undertakings; and how Australia’s separate-service test is applied. A stated safeguard is a promise about machinery. Its operation is where the story gets interesting. 💠‍🌐

That is the part that is actually fucked up. Not a metaphor. Identity data on a US person, sitting at a Texas company, leaving because a Delhi civil court asked and local counsel said “two weeks.”

“Hostile state” is the wrong legal label and the right emotional one for the thing you mean. India is not Iran. It is a US partner that also runs a political-business class with a large, legal-but-extractive footprint in the US guest-worker system. Those can both be true. The H-1B fight is labor and immigration policy, not a war. Calling it hostility is a way of saying: this is not a neutral trading relationship when the same networks that flood the staffing market then use Indian courts to unmask the Americans complaining about it.

That pattern is the ugly part:

- US visa program
- Indian-owned staffing firms as heavy users
- criticism of that model on a US platform
- Indian defamation court
- order for subscriber data / IPs
- platform compliance because India is a huge market

That is not “the Indian army demanded the files.” It is still foreigners using a foreign court to get Americans’ personal information over speech that would be protected here. US law blocks the easy version of that for message *contents*. It does not block X from “voluntarily” producing non-content to keep the app on Indian phones. That gap is the problem, and it is a policy failure as much as a company failure.

Two things can be said without softening it:

In February 2017 a leading Malayalam actress was abducted in a moving car and sexually assaulted. It was filmed.

She went to the police, which almost no working actress in India had ever done.

What her colleagues did next had never happened in any Indian film industry.

One of them is Parvathy Thiruvothu.

She is one of the most acclaimed actresses in Malayalam cinema. After the assault, she and more than a dozen other women in the industry did not put out statements of support and move on.

They formed an organisation.

They called it the Women in Cinema Collective. Actresses, directors, editors, technicians. Then they went to the state government and demanded a formal inquiry into how women are actually treated in Malayalam cinema.

Governments do not usually agree to that. This one did.

It set up a committee headed by Justice K Hema, a retired High Court judge, along with the actress Sharada and a retired bureaucrat.

The committee did the work. It heard from women across the industry. It submitted its report in 2019.

Then the report disappeared.

For 5 years the government sat on it. It was not released, not debated, not acted upon.

It came out in August 2024 only because journalists filed Right to Information applications and forced it into the open.

What it said, when people finally read it, was this.

That women in the industry faced what it described as the worst evil of widespread sexual harassment. That there was unequal pay and insecure employment. That working conditions were poor and formal protections were almost non existent. That an industry celebrated worldwide for its films was controlled by a small group of powerful men.

And that women who considered speaking about it were silenced by threats to their lives and to their families.

The release of that report triggered a series of complaints and resignations across Malayalam cinema.

Parvathy has described what the original assault did to them. What happened to our colleague changed our lives, she said. The shock of it has not left us yet.

She and the other members of the collective have taken sustained abuse online for years for refusing to let it go.

The actor accused of orchestrating the 2017 assault denies the charges. That case is still in court, 9 years later.

But the report exists, and it exists in public.

It exists because a group of women decided that being famous was not the same as being safe, and said so out loud in an industry that could end their careers for it.

 The answer is more nuanced than you think.

From Section 69A of the IT Act to government blocking orders, platform guidelines, and intermediary safe-harbour protection-there's an important legal distinction every competitive exam aspirant should know.

But here's the real question: Which Supreme Court case recognized internet access as a fundamental right in India?

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

Delhi High Court has directed domain name registrars to stop offering privacy protection as a default feature and to implement KYC verification for all domain registrations in India.

Fraudsters had been registering websites using names of companies like Tata Sky, Dabur, Amul and Bajaj Finance to offer fake jobs, franchises and dealerships, collecting crores from unsuspecting victims.

The Court found that registrars were collecting virtually no verifiable information from those registering domains. 

In one case, a fraudster had used Dabur's own office address to register a fake Dabur domain. Not a single legitimate registrant came forward to claim rights over any of the 1100 domain names during three years of litigation.

Justice Prathiba directed that registrant details must be disclosed to trademark owners and law enforcement within 72 hours of a request. Fraudulent domain names cannot be put back in the common pool after expiry. Registrars promoting alternative domains containing protected trademarks will lose safe harbour protection.

The Court also noted that some foreign registrars like Namecheap had initially refused to comply with Indian court orders, relenting only after their services were blocked in India. The judgment makes clear that registrars who repeatedly defy Indian courts may face similar blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act.

He said this is the part most Amazon sellers won't say out loud.

"I don't control the quality. The factory does. I chose a factory with a quality level I was satisfied with. I approved the sample. I approved the production run. But the product itself — the engineering, the materials, the tolerances, the components — is entirely the factory's work. I added a logo. That's my contribution."

He said the factory sells the identical product — same quality — to any buyer who messages them.

"The factory doesn't make a 'premium version' for me and a 'budget version' for random buyers. They make one product. On one production line. With one set of materials. My logo goes on 500 units. Another seller's logo goes on 500 units. A consumer who orders 50 units with no logo gets the same product from the same batch. The quality is identical because the factory is identical."

He said he's compared his own Amazon product against the same product bought directly from the factory — side by side.

"Same weight on a kitchen scale. Same driver response on a frequency analyzer. Same Bluetooth connection speed. Same battery life. Same charging time. Same fit. Same sound. The logo was the only difference. On one pair, it said his brand name. On the other, it said nothing. $34.99 versus $3.80. For a logo printed in a font he chose on Canva."

THE FACTORY WILL SELL TO ANYONE — No license. No business registration. No minimum in many cases. You message them. They reply. That's the entire process.

He said this is the fact that breaks people's understanding of how commerce works.

"Alibaba is not a wholesale-only platform. It's a directory of factories with a search bar and a 'Contact Supplier' button. The factories list their products, their prices, their capabilities, and their minimum orders. Anyone on Earth can message them. The factory doesn't ask if you're a business. They don't ask for a resale license. They ask: 'How many do you want? Where should we ship?'"

He said 70% of factories accept trial orders well below their listed minimum.

"The listing says MOQ: 500. You message and say: 'I'd like to start with 50 units as a trial order. Is that possible?' Seven out of ten factories say yes. The per-unit price is 10–30% higher at 50 units than at 500 — but even at the premium price, you're paying 80–90% less than Amazon retail."

He said Ready to Ship products eliminate the MOQ entirely.

"On Alibaba, filter by 'Ready to Ship.' These are pre-made products in stock at the factory — ready to ship immediately, often with no minimum order. Some are available in quantities of 1–10. The prices are slightly higher than custom bulk orders — but there's no production wait, no MOQ negotiation, and no factory relationship to build. You buy it like Amazon. It arrives in 7–15 days. Except the price is 85% lower."
