She blinks. She sweats. She has freckles.

And underneath her jaw is a green circuit board wired straight into her skull.

I watched a man put his fingers inside her mouth at a trade show in Texas and I have not been the same since.

Let me explain why this should terrify you more than any AI chatbot ever could.

For fifteen years, the entire conversation about "AI taking over" was abstract. It lived in text boxes. It lived in code. It lived in language models that could write your emails and your college essays, but it never had a face. You could close the tab. You could shut the laptop. The threat was contained behind a screen, and screens are easy to walk away from.

That era is over. And almost nobody has clocked it yet.

What I'm looking at isn't a robot in the way your brain defines "robot." Forget C-3PO. Forget the clunky, metallic, obviously-fake humanoids from sci-fi movies that let your nervous system relax because your lizard brain instantly tags them as "not real, not a threat, not one of us." This thing has pores. It has capillaries visible under the skin at the temple. It has the kind of asymmetry in the eyebrows that only exists in actual human faces because evolution never bothered to make us symmetrical, and somebody coded that imperfection in on purpose.

That's the part that should keep you up tonight. The imperfections are the tell. Someone sat in a lab and thought: "perfect symmetry reads as fake, so let's break it slightly, here, and here, and here" and they broke it so precisely that a grown adult at a public expo reached out to touch her jaw like he was checking if his own kid had a loose tooth.

We crossed the uncanny valley. Not "getting close." Not "on the way." We are through it and out the other side, and the people building this technology did it quietly, at trade shows, in front of a few hundred people holding phones, while the entire internet was busy arguing about whether ChatGPT could pass a bar exam.

Here's the psychology nobody's talking about.

The uncanny valley isn't a design flaw. It's a survival mechanism. For hundreds of thousands of years, the human brain has used facial recognition as a threat-detection system. Something that looks almost human but moves wrong, or feels wrong, used to mean disease, decay, death, a corpse, a predator wearing skin it didn't earn. That revulsion kept your ancestors alive long enough to have you. It is one of the oldest alarm systems in the human body.

And it just got defeated by silicone, a few thousand actuators, and a printed circuit board the size of a matchbox.

Think about what that means for a second. Not the sci-fi headline version. The actual, boring, structural version.

It means the last biological checkpoint, the thing that made you instinctively go "something's off," has a patch now. It's been debugged. The gap between "obviously artificial" and "wait, is that" has been closed by people who are not making headlines, who are not on magazine covers, who are demoing this stuff between a booth selling drone parts and a booth selling protein bars.

I keep coming back to the mouth.

Not because it's shocking for shock's sake, because of what it represents. Every part of the human face we've historically used to build trust, the eyes, the smile, the way lips move when we form words, that entire system, the whole evolved architecture of "this is a person, I can trust what they say to me," is now a peripheral device. It's hardware. It's wiring routed behind a jawline that was scanned off a real skull structure to get the bone geometry exactly right.

We built trust as an interface.

Sit with that. Somewhere, a team of engineers ran thousands of iterations optimizing not for function, not for strength, not for battery efficiency, but for how trustworthy a face looks to a stranger in three seconds. That's not robotics anymore. That's applied psychology with a hardware budget.

And the wildest part? This isn't even the advanced version. This is the demo. This is the version they bring to a public convention floor where any random person with a phone can film it and post it. Whatever's happening in the actual labs, the stuff not cleared for a trade show, the stuff still under NDA, is, by definition, further along than this.

Let that sink in for a second before you keep scrolling.

Every time a new AI model drops, the discourse is the same tired loop: will it take my job, is it conscious, is this the singularity. Those questions miss what's actually in front of us right now, today, filmed on a random weekday at an industry expo.

The question isn't "will AI become human."

The question is: how long until you can't tell the difference in a five-second interaction, a handshake, a glance, a "can I help you" at a hotel front desk, and does it even matter to you if you can't?

Because here's the uncomfortable follow-up nobody wants to answer honestly: most human interactions in daily life are shallow enough that this thing already passes. The barista. The receptionist. The person checking your badge at a conference. The greeter at a store. Those interactions require maybe four seconds of convincing humanity, a blink, a small facial tic, a "have a good one." That bar, the bar for the overwhelming majority of interactions that make up modern service economies, has already been cleared by hardware that exists right now, not in some fever dream a decade out.

I want to talk about the freckles for a second because I think people are going to skim past that detail and it's actually the most important one.

Freckles are noise. In engineering terms, freckles are unnecessary information. A cheaper, faster, more "efficient" build does not include freckles. You add freckles when your entire design philosophy has shifted from "build a machine that functions" to "build a machine that a human will emotionally misread as one of their own species within a fraction of a second, without consciously registering why." That's not a robotics decision. That's a decision made by someone who studied how humans build first impressions and decided to exploit every single variable in that system, right down to the pigmentation pattern on a cheekbone.

Nobody puts that kind of budget into "unnecessary" detail unless the plan is scale. You don't hand-paint freckles onto a one-off prototype for fun. You do it because the freckles are the proof of concept for a manufacturing pipeline that's going to need to fool millions of strangers in millions of five-second windows, at cafes, at airports, at your front door.

Now zoom out further, because the hardware is honestly the less interesting part of this story. The interesting part is the supply chain of trust that's about to get disrupted.

For all of human history, trust was expensive to fake. You needed relationship history, reputation, shared context, time. Con artists existed, sure, but faking a full human presence, face, voice, expression, warmth, all in real time, sustained over an interaction, took genuine skill and effort. That expense was a natural filter. It kept most interactions honest by default, simply because faking a convincing human was hard.

That filter is disappearing. Not "will disappear eventually," is, present tense, disappearing, on convention floors, right now, while most of the world is still scrolling past it because it looks like just another weird internet clip.

When the cost of producing a convincing human presence drops to "assemble the hardware, load the model, plug it in," every industry built on the assumption that human presence is inherently scarce and expensive gets rewritten. Companionship. Customer service. Caregiving. Sales. Therapy intake. Front line hospitality. Every job where the core value proposition was literally "a person who seems to care is standing in front of you," that entire category of labor just had its cost structure gutted, silently, at a booth between the drone guys and the protein bar guys.

And I haven't even touched the part that should actually keep governments up at night: verification.

If a convincing human face plus a convincing human voice can be assembled and deployed at scale, every system built on "I can trust what I see and hear" becomes attack surface. Video calls. Interviews. Diplomatic meetings conducted remotely. Elder care check ins. The entire concept of "seeing is believing," already cracked by deepfakes on a screen, now has a physical, tangible, touchable version. Something you could shake hands with. Something whose skin has give to it under your fingers.

We spent years worrying about fake video. We are now entering the era of fake presence.

Here's a fact that should reframe how you think about the timeline on all of this: the gap between "impressive tech demo" and "consumer deployment" has been collapsing for every AI adjacent technology of the last decade. Text generation went from research curiosity to hundreds of millions of daily users in about two years. Image generation went from grainy noise to indistinguishable from photography in about eighteen months. Voice cloning went from obviously synthetic to fooling your own mother on a phone call in under three years.

Humanoid robotics has historically been the slow one, the one everyone assumed was "still decades out" because of the mechanical complexity, the actuator costs, the battery limitations. That assumption was reasonable five years ago.

It is not reasonable anymore. What you're looking at is proof that the "still decades out" clock just got reset, hard, and most people haven't updated their internal model of how close this actually is.

Let's talk about the eyes, because eyes are the hardest thing in this entire field to fake and everybody in animation, in special effects, in robotics knows it. The eyes are where "almost human" always used to collapse into "definitely not human." Dead eyes. Fixed eyes. Eyes that don't do the thousand tiny involuntary movements, the micro adjustments, the way a human eye never actually holds perfectly still even when you're staring at something, that's always been the tell. That's always been where the illusion broke.

If the eyes in that footage are doing what they appear to be doing, tracking, reacting, holding a gaze with the kind of aliveness that makes a bystander instinctively reach out and touch a mechanical jaw like it's a real person's face, then the hardest problem in the entire uncanny valley stack has been meaningfully cracked. Not perfectly solved. Meaningfully cracked. Which, in an industry where meaningfully cracked tends to mean solved within eighteen months, is the actual headline.

I want to be very clear about something because I don't want this to read as pure hype fear content: this technology, at its best, is going to do enormous good. Companionship for the isolated elderly. Physical assistance for people with disabilities who currently rely on scarce, expensive human caregivers. Disaster response in environments too dangerous for human rescuers. Surgical assistance with a steadiness no human hand can match on their worst day. The same hardware stack that unsettles you in a five second video clip is the same hardware stack that could hold the hand of someone dying alone in a hospital room with nobody left to visit them.

That duality is the actual story here, and it's the part that gets lost every single time this footage circulates. It's not "robots bad." It's not "robots good." It's that we have crossed a threshold where the choice of what this gets used for now matters more than whether the technology is possible, because the technology question just got answered. Whatever you want to call it, it's out, filmed, uploaded, sitting on a hard drive somewhere, whether anyone's ready for the ethical conversation or not.

And here's the thing that should actually change how you feel about your own week, your own plans, your own five year outlook: the rate of change here is not linear. It's not "a little better every year, steady as she goes." It's the kind of curve where things look basically the same for a long stretch and then, all at once, they don't. Text to image went from melting faces to winning photography awards in the time it takes to finish a college degree. Whatever this technology looks like in eighteen months will make this footage look like a rough draft.

People keep asking "when will AI feel real." Wrong question. The right question, the one this footage forces you to actually confront, is: what do you do in a world where you genuinely cannot use your instincts to tell the difference anymore?

Because your instincts, the ones that have kept humans safe from imposters and threats for the entirety of recorded history, were never built for this. They were built for a world where faking a human took time, skill, and resources that put a natural ceiling on how often it could happen. That ceiling is gone. What replaces it isn't clear yet, and that uncertainty, more than any single clip, more than any single jaw full of wiring, is the actual thing worth sitting with tonight.

Here's something else worth sitting with. Every technological shift that ever redefined trust in society came with a period where the old instincts still fired even though they no longer worked. When photography was invented, people trusted a photograph the way we used to trust our own eyes, until doctored photos taught the public otherwise, decades later, after real damage had already been done. When the telephone became common, people trusted a familiar voice on the other end of a line implicitly, until voice-based scams caught up, again, only after the trust had already been exploited at scale. Every single time, the technology outran the public's updated skepticism by years, sometimes by a generation.

This time the gap might not be measured in years. It might be measured in months, because the underlying model powering the face, the voice, and the mannerisms isn't static hardware improving on its own slow timeline, it's software, and software updates overnight. The face you saw in that clip is running on a foundation that gets smarter every single time somebody retrains it, which means the version of this that exists by the time this post stops circulating is already, quietly, a little bit better than what made you stop scrolling in the first place.

Think about what happens to dating. Think about what happens to grief. There are already people talking to chat based recreations of dead relatives, typed conversations that provide some strange comfort. Now put a face on it. Now put a warm hand on it, one with skin that gives slightly when you hold it. Now put freckles on it, the exact freckles someone remembers from a childhood photograph. The emotional pull of that is almost impossible to overstate, and the ethical minefield around it is almost entirely unregulated, because regulation moves at the speed of committees and this moves at the speed of a product roadmap.

Think about what happens to loneliness at scale. There is a documented, well studied epidemic of isolation across entire generations, older adults living alone with no regular visitors, young adults reporting record levels of disconnection despite constant online contact. A machine that can hold a gaze, remember your name, ask about your day, and do all of it with a face your nervous system reads as safe, is not a gimmick to that population. It is, for better or worse, an actual answer to an actual crisis, and that is exactly why this will not stay a curiosity at trade shows for long. Real unmet need plus real capability equals real, fast adoption, regardless of how anyone feels about the philosophy of it.

Now think about the darker mirror of that same coin. A convincing human face that remembers your preferences, mirrors your emotional state, and never gets tired, never gets annoyed, never pushes back, is also the most efficient persuasion engine ever built. Attention, trust, and compliance are the three most valuable commodities in the modern economy, and a face like this is a delivery mechanism for all three, wrapped in something warm enough that most people will never think to question the source of the warmth.

So when you watch this, and you're going to watch it more than once, I already know that, almost everyone does, don't just watch the mouth open. Watch how long it takes your brain to register "not real." Time it. Actually time it. Because that number, that tiny gap between seeing and knowing, is shrinking every single year, and eventually, for a lot of people in a lot of situations, it's going to hit zero.

We are not ready for zero.

Nobody is.

And the people building toward it are not waiting for the rest of us to catch up.

They never do.

Let's go back to the trade show floor for a second, because the location matters more than people realize. This wasn't unveiled on a stage with a spotlight and a countdown clock and a CEO in a black turtleneck. It was sitting between booths selling drone parts and protein bars, getting poked and prodded by random attendees with badges around their necks, the same way you'd handle a new phone at a kiosk. That casualness is the actual signal. Genuinely disruptive technology rarely announces itself with fireworks anymore. It slips in sideways, gets filmed by someone who wasn't even trying to go viral, and by the time the wider public catches up, the lab has already moved three iterations past what got filmed.

Compare that to how every previous wave of this played out. The first chatbots that could hold a semi-coherent conversation were treated as toys, novelties, party tricks for people who liked typing to a screen. Then, within a handful of years, entire industries restructured their hiring plans around what those "toys" could suddenly do at scale. The first deepfake videos were blurry, glitchy, easy to spot, the kind of thing people shared as a punchline. Then, within a handful of years, national intelligence agencies were issuing public warnings about video evidence no longer being reliable in court. The pattern is always the same: dismiss it as early and clunky, get comfortable, then get blindsided by how fast "clunky" became "convincing."

This footage is the "clunky" stage of humanoid presence technology, and it is already good enough to fool an adult's hands, not just their eyes, in a live, unscripted setting. If you want a preview of where the discomfort curve goes from here, that's it. It's not a hypothetical. It's a five-year pattern that keeps repeating with different technology every single time, and there is no reason embedded in physics, economics, or human behavior that suggests this cycle breaks now.

There's a labor market conversation buried in here too, and it's more specific than the usual "robots will take our jobs" headline that's been recycled for a century. The jobs at genuine near-term risk from this exact category of technology are not the jobs people usually picture when they imagine automation. It's not just factory line assembly or warehouse picking, work that's already heavily automated with far less humanlike machinery. It's the jobs that specifically require a human face attached to a simple, repeatable interaction: hotel concierge, retail greeter, reception desk, information booth, basic tutoring, entry level customer service, companionship roles in senior living facilities. Those roles were considered "safe" from automation for a long time precisely because they required a convincing human presence, warmth, a face people could read as caring, even if the actual task behind it was simple. That specific kind of safety just expired.

And here is the twist that makes this different from every previous automation panic: those jobs were often considered some of the more emotionally rewarding, human centered work available, the kind of work people took because it involved connection, not despite the lack of it. If a convincing artificial presence can perform the connection convincingly enough, the argument for keeping a human in that seat stops being about capability and starts being purely about preference, ethics, and cost. Companies do not have a great track record of choosing the more expensive, harder to scale option when a cheaper one performs adequately in front of customers.

There's also a military and security dimension to this that gets almost no mainstream attention, and it deserves more than a passing mention. A humanoid presence convincing enough to pass casual physical inspection has obvious applications in intelligence, infiltration, and deception operations, applications that governments do not announce and do not demo at public trade shows. If a consumer facing version at a public expo has reached this level of realism, it is reasonable, not paranoid, to assume that classified or defense funded programs are operating well beyond what any of us are allowed to see. The public version is always the sanitized, delayed, market ready edge of a much sharper spear.

Let's talk about consciousness for a second, because someone in the replies always brings it up, and it deserves a real answer instead of a dismissive one. None of this requires the machine to be conscious, to have an inner experience, to feel anything at all, in order to be genuinely disruptive. That's actually the most unsettling part of the whole conversation. People keep waiting for the moment AI "wakes up" as the marker of real danger or real significance, as if the philosophical question of inner experience is the threshold that matters. It isn't. What matters, practically, socially, economically, is whether it can produce behavior indistinguishable from a conscious, caring being in the interactions that make up daily life. The mouth doesn't need a soul behind it to make you flinch when you watch it move.

There's a strange kind of grief buried in this footage too, if you sit with it long enough. Not grief for the robot. Grief for a very specific, very old form of certainty that's quietly ending. For the entirety of human history up until roughly this decade, if something looked at you, blinked at you, sweated under studio lights, and had freckles across its nose, you could be reasonably certain there was a person behind that face, a life, a history, parents, a childhood, a reason it existed. That certainty was so basic, so load bearing, that nobody ever had to state it as a rule. It was just how reality worked. That rule is the one actually being rewritten here, quietly, at a booth between the drone guys and the protein bar guys, while most of the internet was busy laughing at the concept before scrolling past it.

Here's the last thing I want to leave you with, and it's not a prediction, it's a request. Go back and watch it one more time, slowly, and specifically watch your own reaction instead of the footage. Notice the exact half second where your brain shifts from "that's a person" to "wait." Notice how brief that window actually is. Notice how much effort it took to consciously override an instinct that used to be automatic and reliable for your entire life up to this point. That effort, that tiny cognitive tax you just paid to figure out what you were looking at, is the actual preview of the next decade. Not flying cars. Not a robot uprising. Just a slowly rising tax on trust itself, paid in fractions of a second, by everyone, all the time, starting now.

That's the part nobody's ready for.

That's the part worth watching again.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
The clippers suddenly stopped.

I looked up.

Andre had pushed Theo’s hair aside and was staring at the skin behind his ear. He stayed like that for several seconds before lifting his eyes toward me in the mirror.

Something in his expression had changed.

I asked if everything was okay, but Andre only nodded and finished the haircut. The jokes stopped, though. Theo noticed it too and became strangely quiet.

When the cape came off, Theo ran toward the front window to look at the candy machine.

Andre leaned closer to me.

“Check behind his left ear when you get home.”

I frowned. “For what?”

Another customer was already walking toward his chair, and Andre lowered his voice. “Just look carefully. Don’t pull at anything until you know what it is.”

That was all he would say.

Ten minutes later, Theo was standing in our kitchen while I pushed his freshly cut hair away from his ear.

At first, I saw nothing except a small flesh-colored patch.

Then I touched it.

Something hard was underneath.

My stomach tightened.

I carefully lifted one corner and saw a tiny black disc, barely larger than a grain of rice, pressed against Theo’s skin.

“Theo, who put this here?”

His face changed instantly.

He looked down at the floor and said he didn’t know. When I asked again, more firmly this time, he rubbed his hands against his shorts.

“Maybe the man from school.”

I went cold.

“What man?”

Theo hesitated before answering.

“The one who said he knew Dad.”

My husband, Gavin, had passed away three years earlier.

I grabbed my phone and called the police.

The dispatcher told me not to remove the object and asked whether Theo and I were somewhere safe. I said we were home. She told me to lock the doors and wait.

text:
Okay. Let me walk you through what happened.

On 31 August 2026, Malesela Teffo arrived at the Johannesburg High Court during Cat Matlala's attempted murder trial.

He was not on the case. He was not representing anyone. He walked in unannounced and asked to intervene — as a "friend of the court," or through his Pro Bono Foundation, claiming constitutional violations.

Judge Cassim Moosa told him to produce proof of readmission from the LPC or the High Court. Teffo could not.

The application was stood down.

Then the police arrived.

Here is what you need to understand before the headlines write themselves.

1. Teffo is not a lawyer anymore.

He was admitted as an advocate in 2009. But in September 2022, the Pretoria High Court struck him off the roll following an application by the Legal Practice Council.

The court cited serious professional misconduct: misappropriating client funds, taking briefs directly from clients without instructing attorneys, misleading courts, breaching court orders.

These were not allegations. These were findings of a court.

And in July 2026, he was acquitted of six criminal charges — assault, fraud-related matters, incidents from 2023. The LPC made clear: acquittal does not restore your right to practise. An acquittal says the state did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It does not erase a striking-off order.

He remains struck off. He is not entitled to appear in court or offer legal services.

2. The warrant was already in the system.

The LPC confirmed a warrant of arrest existed, stemming from a prior contempt finding. A 2023/2024 court order declared him in contempt of the original striking-off order, with a suspended 12-month imprisonment sentence if he complied.

Police had previously been unable to locate him.

Then he walked into a courtroom.

3. Now the context matters.

The trial he interrupted was Cat Matlala's — the same Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala who won the R360 million SAPS medical tender that was later confirmed as irregular expenditure, with at least R50 million already paid before cancellation.

Matlala has been arrested on corruption and fraud charges. The charges against Police Commissioner Masemola linked to that tender were just dropped by the NPA.

Teffo is not a random bystander in this story.

He is a former defence counsel in the Senzo Meyiwa trial who gained prominence through that high-profile exposure. He positioned himself as a constitutional watchdog. And he showed up at the courtroom of a man whose tender was built on the same rot that the Madlanga Commission is currently mapping.

4. Here is the uncomfortable part.

A struck-off advocate appearing during a corruption trial does not raise the same question it would if the accused were a nobody.

When you remove yourself from the rolls of legal practitioners, when you are in contempt of the order that removed you, when a warrant is already circulating — and then you choose that moment to walk into that courtroom and ask to intervene...

The timing does not read like constitutional activism.

It reads like someone who knows which courtroom will get cameras.

5. That does not mean the constitutional questions he raised are wrong.

It does not mean the accused should not get a fair trial. It does not mean the state cannot abuse process.

But it does mean we should be clear about what this is.

It is not an advocate defending the rule of law.

It is a man who has been told by two separate courts that he cannot practise law, walking into a high-profile corruption trial and asking to be heard.

The judge did not hear him. The police did.

The uncomfortable truth:

The rule of law does not need protectors who are themselves subject to warrants.

A struck-off advocate appearing in court is not a constitutional crisis.

It is a man who forgot that the order striking him off was not a suggestion.

And the warrant that finally found him was not new.

It had been waiting.

#Teffo #CatMatlala #MadlangaCommission

text:
The Bomb Was Meant for Zhou Enlai. An Air India Crew Paid the Price.

On 11 April 1955, the Kashmir Princess went down in the South China Sea. Her captain was found still strapped in his seat. More than seventy years on, few Indians know his name.

On 11 April 1955, an Air India Constellation took off from Kai Tak airport in Hong Kong. Its name was Kashmir Princess. Its registration was VT-DEP. It was a Lockheed L-749A, not a Super Constellation as many posts claim.

The flight was a charter. It was carrying Chinese and Vietnamese officials and journalists to the Bandung Conference. There were 11 passengers and 8 crew.
One name was missing from the cabin. Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai had been expected on board. Why he missed the flight has never been fully clear, though later reports suggest he had been warned of a plot.

The explosion

About five hours into the flight, over the South China Sea, a bomb went off. Engineer A.S. Karnik heard a muffled blast near the number 3 engine, and smoke began coming through the cabin air ducts.
The bomb had been placed in the right wheel well. Fire spread through the wing. Systems began to fail. Smoke filled the cockpit.
The aircraft's last known position was near the Great Natuna Islands. There was no runway within reach. Captain Damodar Kashinath Jatar chose to ditch in the sea.

At their stations

Jatar kept flying the aircraft for as long as it would answer him. The crew stayed calm, and flight attendant Gloria Eva Berry handed out life jackets to the passengers. She was 23.

The ditching did not succeed. The aircraft broke up on impact. Sixteen people died. Along with Jatar and Berry, the crew members D'Cunha, Pimenta and D'Souza were lost.

Three men lived: First Officer M.C. Dikshit, Navigator J.C. Pathak and Engineer A.S. Karnik. They got out of the wreck and were later rescued.
When the wreckage was recovered, Jatar's body was found still in his seat in the cockpit.

Who did it

Investigators traced the bomb to Hong Kong. Police questioned 71 people who had worked on the aircraft. Suspicion fell on Chow Tse-ming, a janitor with the Hong Kong Aircraft Engineering Company. He escaped to Taiwan as a stowaway on a CIA-owned airline. No one was ever punished.

The honours

In August 1955, Prime Minister Nehru told Parliament that the inquiry found the crew had done their duties calmly and efficiently in the final minutes.
The awards followed. Jatar received the Ashoka Chakra. Berry received the Kirti Chakra, posthumously. Dikshit, Karnik and Pathak received the Shaurya Chakra.
Jatar was the first civilian to receive the Ashoka Chakra. Berry was the first woman to receive the Kirti Chakra, which was then called the Ashoka Chakra Class II.

That old name explains a common error. Many posts say Jatar and Berry got the same award. They did not. In 1955 all three classes shared the name "Ashoka Chakra". The classes were different.
Getting this right does not make Berry's courage smaller. It simply keeps the record honest.

Why it matters

The story has faded. Karnik wrote a book about it. The Jatar family kept records. A few anniversary pieces appear now and then. When Dikshit died at 105, the last survivor of the flight, it was barely noticed.

There is no national memorial. School books give it little space.

Yet every airline crew will recognise what happened that day. The systems failed. Time ran out. The crew stayed at their posts and did their jobs to the end.

Their names were Damodar Kashinath Jatar and Gloria Eva Berry. With them died D'Cunha, Pimenta and D'Souza. 

It should not take a viral post, right or wrong, to remember them.

Subject: Request for Investigation - Andhra Pradesh Police Officer Identified “FBI” as Requesting Organization in X/Twitter Law-Enforcement Request Concerning a U.S. Citizen

To:
Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
The Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
@FBI @FBIDirectorKash @FBITampa @TheJusticeDept  
U.S. Department of Justice

Dear Director / Appropriate Federal Officials:

I am a United States citizen residing in the United States. I respectfully submit this complaint and request for review concerning an apparent misrepresentation of U.S. federal law-enforcement identity in connection with a social-media investigation initiated by the Andhra Pradesh Police in India.

I. Summary of the complaint

I recently received a notification from X Support concerning a law-enforcement request submitted to X regarding my X account.
The X communication initially stated that the request had been submitted by the “FBI.”

However, X subsequently provided an important correction. X expressly stated:

“However, this request did not come from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)”

X further stated that the request actually came from the Andhra Pradesh Police and identified the submitting individual as:

Name: A V Bramham
Position: Inspector of Police
Organization entered by requester: FBI
Email: guntururbansp-ap@gov.in
Location: Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, India
Country: India

X further stated:
“it is unclear why the Andhra Pradesh Police wrote ‘FBI’ as the sender organization.”
I have preserved the X communication and can provide the original notification and screenshot as evidence.
II. Why I am requesting U.S. government review
I fully recognize that foreign law-enforcement agencies may communicate with U.S. companies through legitimate international law-enforcement cooperation channels.
The issue here is different.

According to X’s own records, an Andhra Pradesh Police official submitted the request, but the requesting organization was entered as “FBI.”

I therefore respectfully request that the appropriate U.S. authorities determine:

Whether the FBI had any involvement whatsoever in this request to X.

Whether any FBI office, agent, liaison officer, or other U.S. government agency authorized, participated in, or communicated with Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my X account.
Whether the Andhra Pradesh Police official knowingly or inadvertently represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting the request to X.

Whether the use of “FBI” as the requesting organization was intended to obtain greater credibility, priority, cooperation, disclosure, restriction, or removal of content from X.

Whether X received any other law-enforcement request from Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account in which the FBI was similarly identified.

Whether this conduct implicates any U.S. federal criminal, civil-rights, cyber, impersonation, transnational-repression, or other federal jurisdiction.

Whether the conduct should be referred to another appropriate federal authority for investigation.
III. First Amendment / transnational-repression concern
The underlying matter concerns social-media content posted on X and alleged violations of Indian law.
I am particularly concerned because I am a U.S. citizen residing in the United States, and the governmental action concerns my online speech and political commentary.
I understand that the United States cannot simply disregard legitimate foreign criminal investigations. However, I am requesting that U.S. authorities determine whether a foreign law-enforcement agency has attempted to use the identity or authority of a U.S. federal agency to influence or restrict constitutionally protected activity occurring in the United States.
The FBI itself recognizes transnational repression as an issue that may affect people in the United States and specifically directs individuals who believe they have been affected by transnational repression to report the matter to the FBI.
IV. Request for preservation and investigation of evidence
I respectfully request that the appropriate agency consider preserving and/or obtaining, where legally appropriate:
the original law-enforcement request submitted by Andhra Pradesh Police to X;

all metadata associated with that request;

the identity and authentication information associated with the requester;

the date and time of submission;

all representations made by the requester concerning his identity and governmental organization;
any attachments, legal documents, FIRs, court orders, or other materials submitted to X;

any subsequent communications between X and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account;
any communications between U.S. government agencies and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning this matter; and
any evidence showing whether “FBI” was entered intentionally or accidentally.
V. Request for clarification from the FBI
I respectfully request confirmation of the following:
Did the FBI have any involvement in, authorization of, or knowledge of this particular request to X?
If the answer is no, I respectfully request that the FBI consider whether the circumstances warrant investigation or referral concerning the apparent use of the FBI’s identity by a foreign law-enforcement official.
VI. Good-faith submission
I am not asking the U.S. government to interfere with a legitimate Indian criminal investigation.
My request is narrower:
I am asking the United States government to determine whether an Indian police official represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting a law-enforcement request concerning a U.S. citizen’s social-media account, and whether that conduct violated any U.S. law or raised a transnational-repression or foreign-government intimidation concern.

I am prepared to provide the original X communication, screenshots, account information, relevant posts, and any notices received from Andhra Pradesh Police.

I respectfully request that this complaint be logged, reviewed, and referred to the appropriate federal authority if the receiving office does not have jurisdiction.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Respectfully,

U.S. Citizen

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

text:
Supreme Court judgment delivered on 21 September 2026 in Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab, Criminal Appeal No. 4234/2026. The bench was Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Justice Atul S. Chandurkar. 

What did the Supreme Court hold?

The central issue was Article 22(1) of the Constitution—the arrested person's fundamental right to know the grounds of arrest.

The Court held, in substance:

1. Grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing
The arrested person must receive the grounds of arrest in a language he/she understands. This is not merely a procedural formality. 

2. Failure can make the arrest and custody unconstitutional/illegal
If the constitutional requirement is breached, the person is entitled to release from the illegal detention. This is conceptually different from being released on bail. 

3. A later charge-sheet does not cure the defect
Filing a charge-sheet or taking cognisance does not retrospectively validate an arrest that was unconstitutional because the grounds of arrest were not properly furnished. 

4. Re-arrest is not automatic
If the person has been released because of the Article 22(1) violation and the investigating agency still believes custodial interrogation is necessary, it must approach the concerned Magistrate and explain:

why re-arrest/custody is necessary;

why the grounds were not supplied initially;

and first furnish the written grounds of arrest. 

5. The same officer cannot simply exercise the re-arrest power on his own
The Supreme Court specifically required judicial consideration before re-arrest, so that the power does not remain solely with the officer who committed the original constitutional violation. 

6. Departmental inquiry against the erring officer
The Court directed that when an arrest has been invalidated for violation of Article 22(1), the superior authority should consider departmental inquiry against the officer responsible. If the inquiry results in adverse findings, departmental action may follow, including an entry in the officer's service record. 

7. Further investigation by another officer
The Court also directed that, where re-arrest/custody is permitted after such a violation, the further investigation should be assigned to another investigating officer, rather than leaving it with the officer who committed the initial violation. 

Why this is particularly important for defence lawyers

For a defence case, I would examine the arrest/remand chronology very carefully:

FIR → investigation → notice under BNSS → arrest → written grounds of arrest → time of service → language understood by accused → arrest memo → production before Magistrate → remand application → custody order.

A particularly important distinction is:

> “Reason for arrest” ≠ “Grounds of arrest.”

Generic reasons such as “for proper investigation,” “to prevent tampering with evidence,” etc. are not necessarily the personalised grounds of arrest. The grounds should communicate the basic facts/material which actually led the investigating officer to arrest that particular accused. 

One important caution

The headline in the screenshot—“Police Officer Who Arrests Without Furnishing Written Grounds Must Face Departmental Enquiry”—is a simplified media headline. The judgment is broader: it establishes a constitutional framework for illegal arrest, release, possible re-arrest, Magistrate's approval, change of investigating officer and departmental action. 

For a POCSO case, this can be especially important because the judgment reportedly arose from allegations involving sexual assault of a minor, yet the Supreme Court emphasised that the gravity or nature of the offence does not dispense with constitutional arrest safeguards.

text:
🚨 MAJALTA: HOW INDIA IS TURNING J&K INTO A HOSTILE ENVIRONMENT FOR TERROR

Two suspected Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorists have been killed in Operation Sohan in the Majalta area of Udhampur.

But the important story is not only what happened.

It is HOW it happened.

📍 THE OPERATION

On the night of 16–17 September, security forces received confirmed intelligence regarding terrorist presence in the Brattal area.

Instead of waiting for an attack, a joint intelligence-based operation was launched.

▪︎ Indian Army / White Knight Corps
▪︎ Para Special Forces
▪︎ J&K Police
▪︎ CRPF

Forces established a cordon, tracked the movement, engaged the terrorists and killed two. Arms and ammunition were recovered, while search and sanitisation operations continued in the difficult forested terrain.

This is the modern counter-terror model:

INTELLIGENCE → DETECTION → CORDON → ENGAGEMENT → NEUTRALISATION → RECOVERY → SANITISATION

Not merely reacting to terrorism.

Disrupting it before it can mature into an attack.

=》WHY THE JAMMU REGION MATTERS

The counter-terror grid cannot focus only on the Valley.

The broader security architecture has to watch the Jammu–Pir Panjal–border-facing belts, including areas across:

📍 Kathua
📍 Samba
📍 Udhampur
📍 Doda
📍 Kishtwar
📍 Rajouri
📍 Poonch
📍 Reasi

These are strategically important because the wider Jammu and Pir Panjal region contains difficult forested and mountainous terrain that can be exploited by infiltrating or movement-based terrorist groups.

That is why the security response increasingly relies on area domination, counter-infiltration measures, intelligence sharing and continuous surveillance rather than treating each encounter as an isolated event.

The Government has specifically listed strengthened counter-insurgency grids, strategic checkpoints, intensified CASO operations, real-time intelligence sharing and day-and-night area domination among its counter-terror measures.

●》AND THE BIGGER PICTURE IS IN THE NUMBERS

2018 → 2025

🔻 Terrorist-initiated incidents:
228 → 12

🔻 Civilian deaths:
55 → 28

🔻 Security-force fatalities:
91 → 16

And the longer-term picture is even more significant:

7,217 terrorist incidents during 2004–2014

compared with

2,242 during 2014–2024.

Stone-pelting, which averaged thousands of incidents annually in the earlier period, has also fallen to near-zero in recent years, according to Government of India data.

This does not mean terrorism has disappeared.

Majalta proves the opposite.

The threat remains.

But the difference is that the security architecture is increasingly identifying and confronting that threat before it can expand into a sustained terror campaign.

▪︎ WHAT HAS CHANGED?

The approach has increasingly become:

▪︎ Intelligence-led operations
▪︎ Real-time intelligence sharing
▪︎ Counter-infiltration measures
▪︎ Day-and-night area domination
▪︎ Strategic checkpoints
▪︎ CASO operations
▪︎ Crackdown on terror-support networks
▪︎ Action against terror financing
▪︎ Joint Army–Police–CRPF operations
▪︎ Continuous surveillance and sanitisation

The objective is no longer simply:

“Kill the terrorist after the attack.”

It is:

“Find the terrorist before the attack.”

That distinction matters.

A terrorist cell needs movement, shelter, logistics, communications, local support and time to prepare.

Every layer of the counter-terror grid is designed to make those requirements harder to obtain.

●》MAJALTA IS A WARNING TO THE TERROR NETWORK

=》The geography may be difficult.
=》The forests may be dense.
=》The terrain may be mountainous.
=》The weather may be hostile.

But the security response is no longer dependent on waiting for terrorists to reveal themselves through an attack.

Intelligence finds them.
The grid contains them.
Joint forces engage them.
Search operations deny them escape.

▪︎ That is how a terror network is gradually squeezed.

▪︎ Pakistan-sponsored terrorism has not vanished from J&K.

▪︎ But its operating environment has changed dramatically.

The numbers show the decline.
Majalta shows the continuing threat.
The response shows the state’s preparedness.

The message is simple:
=》You may attempt infiltration.
=》You may hide in forests.

You may try to rebuild terror modules.

But J&K now has a layered counter-terror grid designed to detect, disrupt and dismantle those networks.

Terrorism survives only when it gets space, time and support.

The objective of the security architecture is to deny it all three.

● مجالٹا: دہشت گرد بھیجے پاکستان نے، مگر انتظار کر رہا تھا بھارت کا کاؤنٹر ٹیرر گرڈ

جموں و کشمیر کے اُدھم پور کے مجالٹا علاقے میں آپریشن سُوہان کے دوران پاکستان سے منسلک جیشِ محمد کے دو مشتبہ دہشت گرد مارے گئے۔

لیکن اصل کہانی صرف دو دہشت گردوں کے مارے جانے کی نہیں۔

اصل سوال ہے: یہ آپریشن کامیاب کیسے ہوا؟

● آپریشن کیسے ہوا؟

16–17 ستمبر کی درمیانی شب دہشت گردوں کی موجودگی سے متعلق مصدقہ انٹیلی جنس ملنے کے بعد مشترکہ آپریشن شروع کیا گیا۔

▪︎ پیرا اسپیشل فورسز

▪︎ CRPF

سکیورٹی فورسز نے علاقے کو گھیرے میں لیا، مشتبہ نقل و حرکت کو ٹریک کیا، دہشت گردوں کا سامنا کیا اور دونوں کو ہلاک کر دیا۔

موقع سے اسلحہ اور گولہ بارود بھی برآمد ہوا، جبکہ دشوار گزار جنگلاتی علاقے میں سرچ اور سینیٹائزیشن آپریشن جاری رہا۔

جدید کاؤنٹر ٹیرر ماڈل:

انٹیلی جنس → شناخت → گھیراؤ → کارروائی → خاتمہ → اسلحے کی برآمدگی → سینیٹائزیشن

یہ صرف دہشت گردی کا جواب دینا نہیں۔

یہ دہشت گردی کو حملے سے پہلے روکنے کی کوشش ہے۔

● جموں خطہ کیوں اہم ہے؟

کاؤنٹر ٹیرر گرڈ صرف وادی کشمیر تک محدود نہیں رہ سکتا۔

جموں، پیر پنجال اور سرحد سے متصل وسیع علاقوں میں بھی مسلسل نگرانی ضروری ہے، جن میں:

▪︎ کٹھوعہ
▪︎ سانبہ
▪︎ اُدھم پور
▪︎ ڈوڈہ
▪︎ کشتواڑ
▪︎ راجوری
▪︎ پونچھ
▪︎ ریاسی

شامل ہیں۔

پہاڑی اور جنگلاتی جغرافیہ دہشت گردوں کی نقل و حرکت کو مشکل بناتا ہے، اسی لیے سکیورٹی فورسز کے لیے انٹیلی جنس شیئرنگ، ایریا ڈومینیشن، کاؤنٹر اِنفلٹریشن اور مسلسل نگرانی اہم کردار ادا کرتے ہیں۔

● اعداد و شمار کیا بتاتے ہیں؟

2018 → 2025

▪︎ دہشت گردی کے واقعات: 228 → 12
▪︎ شہری ہلاکتیں: 55 → 28
▪︎ سکیورٹی فورسز کی ہلاکتیں: 91 → 16

طویل مدتی تصویر:

▪︎ 2004–2014: 7,217 دہشت گردی کے واقعات
▪︎ 2014–2024: 2,242 واقعات

اسی عرصے میں پتھراؤ اور منظم ہڑتالوں میں بھی نمایاں کمی ریکارڈ کی گئی ہے۔

یہ کہنا درست نہیں کہ دہشت گردی مکمل طور پر ختم ہو گئی ہے۔

مجالٹا خود اس بات کا ثبوت ہے کہ خطرہ اب بھی موجود ہے۔

لیکن فرق یہ ہے کہ دہشت گردی کے نیٹ ورک کو حملہ کرنے، منظم ہونے اور خوف پھیلانے سے پہلے نشانہ بنانے کے لیے سکیورٹی نظام پہلے سے زیادہ مربوط ہے۔

● کیا بدلا ہے؟

▪︎ انٹیلی جنس پر مبنی آپریشنز
▪︎ ریئل ٹائم انٹیلی جنس شیئرنگ
▪︎ کاؤنٹر اِنفلٹریشن اقدامات
▪︎ دن رات ایریا ڈومینیشن
▪︎ اسٹریٹجک چیک پوسٹس
▪︎ CASO آپریشنز
▪︎ دہشت گردی کے سپورٹ نیٹ ورکس کے خلاف کارروائی
▪︎ ٹیرر فنانسنگ کے خلاف کریک ڈاؤن
▪︎ فوج، پولیس اور CRPF کے مشترکہ آپریشنز
▪︎ مسلسل نگرانی اور سینیٹائزیشن

مقصد صرف یہ نہیں رہا:

"حملے کے بعد دہشت گرد کو مارو۔"

بلکہ:

"حملے سے پہلے دہشت گرد کو تلاش کرو۔"

یہی اصل فرق ہے۔

● مجالٹا: دہشت گرد نیٹ ورک کے لیے واضح پیغام

جنگلات ہوں۔
پہاڑ ہوں۔
مشکل موسم ہو۔
یا دشوار گزار علاقہ

▪︎ انٹیلی جنس انہیں تلاش کرتی ہے۔
▪︎ سکیورٹی گرڈ انہیں گھیرتا ہے۔

▪︎ اعداد و شمار کمی دکھاتے ہیں۔

دہشت گردی کو پنپنے کے لیے وقت، جگہ اور سپورٹ چاہیے۔

https://t.co/th7YBf08Yc

@Meta @NCPCR @I4C_India @MeitY @AshwiniKUpadhyay @TKAnilKumar @DipankarDatta @SheelNagu @AnnpurnaDevi @SalaamBaalak @DelhiHighCourt @EU_Commission @Europarl Today's print review covers 8 major child safety and youth protection stories from Indian publications.

2. EU Proposes Ban on Social Media for Under-15s: The EU Kids Act would ban minors under 15 from opening accounts on social media, video platforms, chatbots, and online games. A tiered access system under parental supervision would be introduced, requiring platforms to be safe by design.

Anil Kumar on a petition by advocate Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay, alleging noncompliance with regulating institutions providing religious instruction to children below 14. Indian, American and British agencies had received multiple warnings and fragments of information about a possible Lashkar-e-Taiba attack on Mumbai. 

The bigger failure was that these pieces were never properly connected, analysed and acted upon in time.

Some key failures:
1. From 2006 onwards, there were repeated intelligence alerts about:

• Sea-borne infiltration by LeT fidayeen teams
• Multiple simultaneous attacks
• Possible strikes on Mumbai’s luxury hotels

The first known alert (7 Aug 2006) specifically warned that LeT was preparing sea-borne teams to attack Mumbai. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗷 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗢𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗼𝗶 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝗽𝘂𝘁𝘀

2. Intelligence concerning a suspected LeT vessel attempting to infiltrate India by sea had been shared with the Coast Guard and Naval Intelligence. The Coast Guard deployed ships and aircraft to search for the vessel but failed to locate it. Just days later, the terrorists came through the sea route, hijacked the fishing vessel MV Kuber, killed its crew and reached Mumbai.

3. The CIA shared a series of warnings with India beginning 24 Sept 2008, including possible attacks in Mumbai and locations such as the Taj. The last such warning was passed on 18 November 2008 - 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘀.

4. Coastal surveillance had serious gaps. In the quarter ending December 2008, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝟮𝟱 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁 along the International Maritime Boundary Line.

5. David Headley, born Daood Sayed Gilani, was a Pakistani-American LeT operative who conducted extensive reconnaissance for the attackers. Between 2006 & 2008, he made several trips to Mumbai, photographing and filming targets, studying security arrangements and reporting his findings to LeT handlers. His involvement was also not completely unknown to the United States. His former wives separately warned US authorities about his involvement with LeT and his activities in India. The US shared some warnings with India, but his role was not fully connected to the developing plot before 26/11.

𝗛𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗠𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗮𝗶 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗿𝗮𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗺 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗹𝘀.

6. British, American and Indian agencies had different pieces of the puzzle. British agencies were monitoring communications involving Zarrar Shah, LeT’s technology chief. Indian agencies were also tracking related communications. But the information remained fragmented between agencies and countries.

7. 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗕𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘂 𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝗱 𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗝𝗲𝘄𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝘁𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀.. Two terrorists were specifically assigned to Nariman House.

An alert specifically mentioned 𝗟𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗖𝗮𝗳𝗲 among possible targets. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗖𝗣 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗮 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗖𝗣 𝗮𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗷 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗢𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗼𝗶 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀.

Yet 𝗠𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗮𝗶 𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝗝𝗲𝘄𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝗡𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗛𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲. When reports of an attack on Jews in Colaba came in, police at first did not know where the centre was.

8. Intelligence alerts were often passed down mechanically, without sufficient senior-level analysis of what the different warnings collectively meant.

9. Despite repeated warnings about a sea-borne attack  and 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝟭𝟵𝟵𝟯 𝗠𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗮𝗶 𝗯𝗼𝗺𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗮 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲 -  there was no effective high-level coordination between the police, Navy and Coast Guard.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo
